CHARLESTON, South Carolina (CNN)  -- Tropical storm Cristobal was forecast to move "parallel and very close" to the North Carolina coast Sunday morning, but the storm is not expected to make landfall along the eastern U.S. shores. Satellite image taken at 1:15 p.m. Saturday shows Tropical Storm Cristobal off the coast of the Carolinas. At 11 p.m. ET Saturday, the center of the storm was about 45 miles southeast of Cape Fear, North Carolina, and about 170 miles southwest of Cape Hatteras, North Carolina. The National Hurricane Center said Cristobal was moving northeast at about 6 mph, with maximum sustained winds of about 45 mph and some higher gusts. "The center of the tropical storm is expected to move parallel and very close to the coast of North Carolina for the next day or so," the NHC said. It is expected to dump between three and five inches of rain along the Carolina coast this weekend, it said. The storm had not strengthened beyond the 45 mph top winds measured earlier on Saturday, according to the NHC. A discussion posted online by NHC forecasters called Cristobal "convectively challenged" and predicted the storm would "become absorbed ahead of an approaching cold front" by late Monday. Although the center of the storm was forecast to remain off the coast through the weekend, tropical storm warnings were in effect from the South Santee River in South Carolina to the North Carolina-Virginia state line, including Pamlico Sound. Flood advisories were posted for coastal counties, and Wilmington, North Carolina, received 2½ inches of rain Saturday, said Stephen Keebler, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service there. Cristobal's winds were not expected to be a problem, Keebler said. "It's some rain and a little bit of relief for the coastal areas and a lot of excitement, but that's about it," he said. The rain bands were weakening as they spun farther inland, providing little relief for parched areas near Interstate 95 in North Carolina, he said. Forecasters predicted up to 5 inches of rain along the North Carolina coast, with heavier amounts in some areas. Eastern North Carolina is under a moderate drought, and areas along South Carolina's northern coast are considered abnormally dry, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. Officials have blamed the persistent drought for a massive wildfire that has burned more than 40,000 acres in eastern North Carolina since it began June 1 with a lightning strike. As Cristobal lurked offshore, the storm was keeping many boaters off the waters -- and surfers in the waves. On North Carolina's Outer Banks, surfers reveled in the waves as the storm churned offshore well to the south. Bradley Rose, a surf instructor at SandBarz in Carolina Beach, North Carolina, said the waves were a bit choppy. "It looks pretty fun out there," Rose said. At the By the Sea Motel in North Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, out-of-state vacationers took to the beach, trying to photograph the outer rain bands of Cristobal, hotel manager Charlie Peterson said. Intermittent rain showers during the afternoon were not enough to chase them away, and there were even brief moments of sunshine. "They've got their cameras set, and they think there is going to be lightning over the water and all," he said. "They have never seen this." Elsewhere Saturday, Hurricane Fausto strengthened far off Mexico's Pacific coast, while Hurricane Bertha, located east of Cape Race, Newfoundland, was downgraded to tropical storm status. Neither of those storms currently threatens land. Bertha had blustered across Bermuda this week, knocking out electricity to thousands there.

Local officials urged residents not to drive through flooded roads and advised tourists to heed beach safety warnings. **CHARLESTON, S.C. — [Date]** — Tropical Storm Cristobal continued to churn offshore of the Carolinas on [day], bringing dangerous surf, gusty winds, bands of heavy rain and a growing rip-current threat to the South Carolina and North Carolina coasts as forecasters urged residents and visitors to stay weather-aware.

According to the National Hurricane Center, Cristobal was located offshore of the southeastern United States as of the latest advisory, with maximum sustained winds near tropical-storm strength and higher gusts. The storm was moving generally parallel to the coastline, close enough to spread squalls and rough marine conditions across the coastal Carolinas but far enough offshore to keep the strongest winds over the Atlantic.

Forecasters said the system’s impacts were already being felt from the Lowcountry to the Outer Banks, with rain bands rotating inland at times and surf building along exposed beaches. While Cristobal was not expected to make a direct landfall in South Carolina based on the latest forecast track, emergency officials warned that even offshore tropical storms can produce life-threatening conditions.

“This is not a storm to ignore just because the center is offshore,” said a Charleston-area meteorologist. “The hazards extend well away from the center, especially along the beaches and in the tidal creeks. Rip currents, rough surf and brief periods of heavy rain are the main concerns right now.”

Along the Charleston waterfront, winds picked up through the morning as low gray clouds streamed in from the Atlantic. At the Battery, waves slapped against the seawall while tourists took photos between passing showers. Several downtown businesses placed sandbags near entrances as a precaution, particularly in areas prone to nuisance flooding during heavy rain and high tides.

“We’ve seen enough of these systems to know that things can change fast,” said James Rutledge, a Charleston resident who lives near the peninsula’s flood-prone lower streets. “If the tide lines up with the rain, it doesn’t take much for water to start coming up through the drains.”

The National Weather Service offices serving Charleston, Wilmington and Newport/Morehead City were monitoring conditions closely, especially for coastal flooding, marine hazards and isolated tornado potential in stronger rain bands. Tropical storms that pass offshore can sometimes spin up quick, weak tornadoes in outer bands, though the greatest risk typically depends on how far inland those bands move.

Beach communities were urging swimmers to stay out of the water as lifeguards reported increasingly hazardous surf. Red flags were flying at several beaches, and local officials warned that rip currents could remain dangerous even after Cristobal begins to pull away.

“At this point, the biggest message is simple: stay out of the ocean,” said a local beach safety official. “You may look at the beach and think it’s manageable, but rip currents can overpower even experienced swimmers.”

On Isle of Palms, Sullivan’s Island and Folly Beach, residents prepared for a messy stretch of weather rather than a major wind event. Patio furniture was secured, boat owners checked lines and visitors weighed whether to cut short beach plans.

“We came down for a long weekend, but the water is too rough for the kids,” said Michelle Alvarez, visiting Charleston with family from Columbia. “We’re going to stay inland today and keep an eye on the forecast.”

Mariners faced some of the most significant hazards. Offshore waters were expected to remain dangerous, with elevated seas, squalls and gusty winds creating hazardous conditions for small craft. The Coast Guard and local harbor officials advised boaters to remain in port until conditions improve.

“Marine conditions will deteriorate quickly in these bands,” said a Charleston-based meteorologist. “You can go from manageable winds to tropical-storm-force gusts in a short period of time, especially offshore and near the mouths of inlets.”

Power outages were not expected to be widespread unless stronger bands moved ashore repeatedly, but utility crews were on standby in parts of the coastal region. Saturated ground and gusty winds can bring down tree limbs, particularly in older neighborhoods with large live oaks and saturated soils.

Emergency management officials said residents should have multiple ways to receive weather alerts, avoid flooded roads and remain cautious during high tide cycles. Drivers were reminded that saltwater flooding can damage vehicles and that road closures may occur with little warning in low-lying areas.

“Turn around, don’t drown applies here too,” said one county emergency official. “It doesn’t have to be a catastrophic flood to put people in danger. A few inches of moving water can create serious problems.”

The National Hurricane Center forecast called for Cristobal to continue tracking offshore, with gradual changes in strength possible depending on wind shear, sea-surface temperatures and the storm’s interaction with a frontal boundary along the East Coast. Forecasters said the system could begin accelerating away from the Carolinas later in the forecast period, but hazardous surf may linger.

In downtown Charleston, many residents were taking the storm in stride but remained cautious. Restaurants and shops remained open in many areas, though some planned to close early if conditions worsened.

“You don’t panic, but you don’t pretend it’s nothing either,” said local shop owner Renee Whitaker. “We’re watching the tide, watching the rain, and we’ll make decisions as we go.”

Officials stressed that the forecast could still shift and encouraged residents to follow updates from the National Hurricane Center, the National Weather Service and local emergency management agencies.

For now, Cristobal’s most immediate threats to the Carolinas are rough surf, dangerous rip currents, gusty rain bands, localized flooding and hazardous boating conditions — impacts that forecasters say can be serious even without a direct hit.

“People tend to focus on the cone and the center point,” the Charleston-area meteorologist said. “But with tropical storms, the impacts are often spread out. If you’re along the coast today, you need to treat the ocean and the weather with respect.”

**Cristobal Brushes Carolina Coast, Bringing Rough Surf, Rain and Vacation Disruptions**

*By Staff Writer*  
*Outer Banks, N.C. —* Tropical Storm Cristobal churned just offshore of the Carolinas this weekend, lashing parts of coastal North and South Carolina with bands of heavy rain, gusty winds and dangerous surf while largely sparing the region from major damage.

The storm, which developed near the Southeast coast, tracked northeastward along the shoreline, close enough to unsettle beach communities from the Grand Strand to the Outer Banks but far enough offshore to prevent the worst of its winds from coming ashore.

According to the **National Hurricane Center**, Cristobal was forecast to continue moving generally northeast, roughly parallel to the Carolina coast, before accelerating away from land into the open Atlantic. Forecasters said tropical-storm-force winds were most likely over the coastal waters and in exposed areas, with the main hazards for land areas being **heavy rainfall, rip currents, rough surf and minor coastal flooding**.

Tropical storm warnings and advisories were posted for portions of the Carolina coastline as emergency officials urged residents and visitors to monitor forecasts and avoid entering the water.

## Rain, Wind and Rip Currents Along the Coast

In **North Carolina**, Cristobal’s outer rain bands swept across coastal counties, with the Outer Banks seeing periods of wind-driven rain, gray skies and choppy seas. Gusts strengthened along exposed beaches, piers and inlets, while ferry schedules and small-craft operations were closely watched because of deteriorating marine conditions.

Beachgoers on Hatteras Island, Ocracoke and other Outer Banks communities encountered red flags and warnings about dangerous rip currents. Local officials said even where skies temporarily brightened, surf conditions remained hazardous.

“This is the kind of storm that can fool people,” one coastal emergency official said. “It may not look dramatic from the beach at every moment, but the ocean is dangerous.”

Low-lying roads in some coastal spots saw ponding from heavy showers, though widespread structural damage was not reported. The storm’s strongest winds stayed offshore, reducing the likelihood of downed trees and power outages compared with a direct landfalling tropical system.

In **South Carolina**, effects were generally lighter but still noticeable, particularly along the Grand Strand and coastal communities near Myrtle Beach. Intermittent rain, gusty breezes and rough surf disrupted beach plans, while lifeguards and local authorities warned swimmers to stay out of the water during periods of elevated rip-current risk.

Mariners were urged to remain in port as seas built offshore. Small craft advisories covered portions of the coast, and charter fishing trips were delayed or canceled in some locations.

## Vacationers Adjust Plans

For many visitors, Cristobal was less a disaster than an unwelcome interruption to peak beach season.

In Myrtle Beach, families who had planned full days on the sand instead crowded restaurants, arcades, outlet stores and hotel lobbies. Some vacationers watched the surf from balconies as waves pounded the shoreline.

“We came for sunshine, but we’re making the best of it,” said one visitor from Ohio, who spent the morning checking weather updates instead of setting up beach chairs. “The kids are disappointed they can’t swim, but at least we’re still at the beach.”

On the Outer Banks, rental-home guests said the storm added a sense of uncertainty to their stay. Some packed groceries and monitored ferry information, while others took photos of the rough ocean from a safe distance.

Local business owners said the storm hurt outdoor activities but did not appear severe enough to drive large numbers of tourists away.

“A rainy day is never good for beach rentals or surf lessons,” said a shop employee in a coastal town. “But restaurants and indoor attractions usually pick up some of that business.”

## National Hurricane Center Outlook

The National Hurricane Center said Cristobal was expected to remain a tropical storm as it moved away from the coastline. The agency’s forecast track kept the center offshore, reducing the risk of a major land impact, but forecasters emphasized that impacts can extend well away from a storm’s center.

Meteorologists warned that bands of rain could continue affecting coastal North Carolina even as the storm pulled northeast. Rainfall totals in some coastal areas were expected to reach several inches, with localized higher amounts possible where bands repeatedly moved over the same locations.

The NHC also highlighted the threat of **life-threatening rip currents**, a common danger from tropical systems that pass offshore. Those currents can persist even after winds decrease and skies clear.

## Broader Tropical Activity in Atlantic and Pacific

Cristobal was part of a busier stretch of tropical weather across both the Atlantic and Pacific basins.

In the Atlantic, forecasters were also monitoring other tropical disturbances, including activity farther south and west in the Caribbean and Gulf region. The National Hurricane Center noted that the warm waters of the western Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico remained capable of supporting additional tropical development as the season progressed.

Elsewhere in the Atlantic basin, prior storm activity had already drawn attention from forecasters, and the emergence of Cristobal near the Southeast coast served as a reminder that tropical systems can form close to land with relatively little advance notice.

In the eastern Pacific, tropical cyclones were also active over open waters. Pacific storms posed little immediate threat to the Carolinas, but forecasters tracked them as part of the broader seasonal pattern of tropical development across the Northern Hemisphere.

## Officials Urge Caution After Storm Passes

Emergency managers along the Carolina coast said the greatest concern remained beach safety. Even after Cristobal’s center moved farther offshore, rough surf and rip currents were expected to linger.

Officials urged visitors to obey flag warnings, avoid swimming when lifeguards advise against it, and keep children away from jetties, piers and inlets where currents are strongest.

“People hear ‘tropical storm’ and think only about wind,” one weather official said. “But with a storm like Cristobal, the ocean is the real danger.”

By late weekend, many coastal communities were already looking ahead to improved conditions, hoping Cristobal’s stay would be brief and its economic impact limited. Still, the storm served as an early-season reminder for residents, vacationers and businesses across the Carolinas: even a glancing blow from a tropical system can disrupt life along the coast.
